newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela closes its most infamous prison.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela closes its most infamous prison.

text.p: Venezuelan authorities on Saturday closed the country's most infamous prison, site of a controversial visit by Pope John Paul II a year ago.
Justice Minister Henrique Meier padlocked the main gate of notoriously violent Catia penitentiary after the last 639 inmates were transferred by bus to another jail.
Located on the north-western outskirts of Caracas, the Reten de Catia had over the years come to symbolise everything that is wrong with Venezuela's crammed, squalid and violent prisons.
Authorities planned to blast the rundown white-brick structure to rubble in the next two weeks, possibly on Feb. 9, exactly one year after the pope's visit.

The pontiff on that date in 1996 blessed what he thought were inmates waving handkerchiefs and Vatican and Venezuelan flags from their cells. The prison's chaplain later said the "inmates" were in fact police officers, causing a major embarrassment to the government.
Commonly referred to as "Hell," the Catia jail was built 35 years ago for 750 inmates but in recent months held more than 2,000. It remained violent until the end.
Prison officials said one prisoner was found dead on Friday night. He had been stabbed fifteen times.

At least 206 prisoners, an average of four a week, were killed last year in Venezuela's 32 jails, which hold 25,000 prisoners. Only one in four inmates has been sentenced. The rest wait, sometimes for years, to be tried.
